title: Probability Distribution
body:
A distribution is the full accounting of how a [[Random Variable]] spreads its probability: which
values, with what weight. Six of them cover almost everything this course does, and **the skill
being taught is not the formulas, it is recognising which family a described situation belongs
to.** This note is that selection table.

## The families

| Family | Discrete? | Answers | Parameters | $E[X]$ | $\text{Var}(X)$ |
|---|:-:|---|---|---|---|
| [[Bernoulli Distribution\|Bernoulli]] | yes | one trial, success or not | $p$ | $p$ | $p(1-p)$ |
| Binomial | yes | successes in $n$ fixed trials | $n, p$ | $np$ | $np(1-p)$ |
| Geometric | yes | trials until the first success | $p$ | $1/p$ | $(1-p)/p^2$ |
| Poisson | yes | events in a fixed interval | $\lambda$ | $\lambda$ | $\lambda$ |
| Uniform | no | every value in $[a,b]$ equally likely | $a, b$ | $(a+b)/2$ | $(b-a)^2/12$ |
| Exponential | no | waiting time until the next event | $\lambda$ | $1/\lambda$ | $1/\lambda^2$ |
| [[Normal Distribution\|Normal]] | no | sums and averages of anything | $\mu, \sigma$ | $\mu$ | $\sigma^2$ |

## The discrete three

**Binomial.** $n$ independent trials, each succeeding with the same probability $p$, count the
successes.

$$
P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}
$$

The formula is readable if you take it apart: $p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$ is the probability of one specific
sequence with $k$ successes, and $\binom{n}{k}$ counts how many such sequences there are. That
binomial coefficient is [[Combination]] from [[DISCRETE MATH]], doing the same job it always does.
Four conditions have to hold, and they are what you check: fixed $n$, two outcomes, constant $p$,
independent trials. Sampling without replacement from a small population breaks the third and
fourth.

**Geometric.** Same trials, but count how many you need until the first success:
$P(X = k) = (1-p)^{k-1}p$. Its defining oddity is **memorylessness**: after ten failures the
distribution of the remaining wait is unchanged. The coin does not owe you anything, and the
gambler's fallacy is the denial of this line.

**Poisson.** Events arriving at an average rate $\lambda$ over a fixed window:

$$
P(X = k) = \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}
$$

Requests per second, defects per metre, keys landing in one hash bucket. It is the binomial's limit
as $n \to \infty$ and $p \to 0$ with $np = \lambda$ held fixed, which is why it fits "many chances,
each unlikely". **Its signature is $\mu = \sigma^2 = \lambda$**, so a sample whose mean and variance
are far apart is not Poisson, and that is a real diagnostic.

## The continuous three

**Uniform** on $[a,b]$: density is the constant $1/(b-a)$, and probability is proportional to
interval width. It is the distribution a random number generator claims to produce, which
[[Random Numbers]] in [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] discusses, and every other distribution is
generated from it by inverting a CDF.

**Exponential**: $f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x \geq 0$, with
$P(X > x) = e^{-\lambda x}$. The waiting time between Poisson events, so the two are one model seen
two ways: Poisson counts arrivals in a window, exponential measures the gap between them. It is the
geometric's continuous twin and it is **memoryless for the same reason**, which is why it models
component lifetimes with no wear-out and models human patience badly.

**Normal**: the bell curve, and it gets its own note. See [[Normal Distribution]].

## Choosing one

```
Counting things?
  fixed number of trials, count successes  -> binomial
  count until first success                -> geometric
  count arrivals in an interval            -> Poisson

Measuring something?
  waiting time to next arrival             -> exponential
  no value preferred over any other        -> uniform
  a sum or an average of many things       -> normal
```

That last line is not a heuristic, it is the [[Central Limit Theorem]], and it is why the normal
shows up for quantities with no obvious reason to be bell shaped: heights are a sum of many small
genetic and environmental contributions, measurement error is a sum of many small errors.

## Related

- [[Random Variable]]: where $E[X]$ and $\text{Var}(X)$ in the table come from
- [[Probability Density Function]]: what the continuous rows mean formally
- [[Bernoulli Distribution]]: the atom the binomial is built from
- [[Normal Distribution]]: the one the rest of the course uses
- [[Hashing]]: keys per bucket under a good hash function is Poisson with
  $\lambda = n/m$, which is where the "expected $O(1)$ lookup" claim actually comes from
- [[Entropy]] and [[KL Divergence]]: functionals of a distribution, so they need this note
